analysis.one_liner: Restricts debt collection tactics, shields medical debt from credit reports, and forgives private student loans at death or disability.
analysis.headline: The House passed it 215-207 on May 13, 2021, but the Senate Banking Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rewritten the rules for debt collection nationwide. It would have forgiven private student loans when a borrower dies or becomes permanently disabled (freeing cosigners, usually parents or relatives), kept most medical debt off credit reports, banned collectors from pursuing debts past the legal deadline, required collectors to document and give notice before suing, and limited texts, emails, and social media messages from collectors. It also extended those rules to debts owed to federal and state agencies and barred certain confession-of-judgment clauses used against small businesses. The House passed it almost entirely along party lines, but the Senate never considered it.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers contacted by debt collectors, people carrying medical bills, private student loan borrowers and the family members who cosigned their loans, servicemembers, and small businesses pressured by confession-of-judgment loan terms.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medical debt holders, student borrowers, servicemembers, small businesses

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders to discharge a private student loan when the borrower dies or becomes totally and permanently disabled, and releases the cosigner instead of pursuing the family.

Bars consumer reporting agencies from including debt from a medically necessary procedure on credit reports, and blocks reporting of other medical debt for at least 365 days, giving people time to settle bills or get insurance or charity care before the debt damages their credit.
Prohibits debt collectors from trying to collect a debt after the statute of limitations has expired, closing a common practice of suing people over old debts they can no longer legally contest.

Requires collectors to send written notice 30 to 60 days before suing, and to file evidence with the lawsuit that they actually own the debt and that the consumer incurred it, against debt-buyer lawsuits built on thin or mistaken records.
Bars collectors from threatening a servicemember with rank reduction, loss of security clearance, or military prosecution to force payment.
Restricts collectors from emailing, texting, or messaging people on social media without their direct consent, and from posting publicly viewable debt demands on social media.

Extends fair-debt-collection rules to debts owed to federal and state agencies, to debt buyers, and to nonjudicial foreclosures, and caps fees charged by collectors of government debts at 10 percent of the amount collected.
Bans lenders from requiring small business borrowers to sign confession-of-judgment clauses, which waive the borrower's right to notice and a day in court before assets are seized.

Provides temporary credit-reporting relief for private student loan borrowers who fell behind during the COVID-19 emergency, and prohibits collecting on medical bills for two years after the first payment is due.
Raises and inflation-indexes the damages consumers can win from violating collectors, and lets courts order collectors to stop violating practices, not just pay fines.

analysis.who_pays: Debt collection firms and debt buyers, the three major credit reporting agencies, private student lenders, and lenders using confession-of-judgment clauses; some costs could surface as tighter credit or higher rates if lenders pass on the added risk.
analysis.who_pays_short: Debt collectors, credit bureaus, private student lenders

drawbacks.text: Mandatory discharge of private student loans at death or disability, and the ban on most medical debt reporting, shift risk onto lenders and furnishers, which an honest supporter should expect to show up as somewhat higher rates or tighter underwriting on private student loans.
The 365-day blackout on medical debt reporting and the two-year collection delay remove information lenders use to price loans, which could make underwriting less accurate for all borrowers.
The bill is paid for by reducing the Federal Reserve's surplus account by $2.9 billion in 2031, a budgetary offset that draws down the central bank's capital rather than raising revenue.

The bill overrides the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's 2021 debt collection rule by directing that no rule may allow unlimited electronic communications, taking the matter out of the regulator's discretion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefits are concrete and go to people in vulnerable moments: a bereaved family no longer hounded for a dead child's student loan, a patient's hospital bill not wrecking their credit score for years, a servicemember no longer threatened with prosecution. The main costs fall on a handful of industries whose business models rely on the practices being restricted, plus some diffuse risk of slightly costlier credit as lenders reprice. The bill is broad and some titles are studies and reports rather than rules, but the operative restrictions target practices with well-documented consumer harm.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it in May 2021, but the Senate Banking Committee never scheduled action on it, and it expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 15, 2021 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee.
The committee marked it up and reported it as amended by a 30-23 committee vote on April 21, 2021.
The House passed the bill on May 13, 2021 by 215-207, with 215 of 218 voting Democrats in favor and none of the 212 voting Republicans in favor.
Republican amendments offered on the floor, including ones by Rep. Wagner, were defeated on recorded votes.
The Senate received the bill on May 17, 2021 and referred it to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee, where no further action was taken before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Debt collectors, private student lenders, and credit bureaus kept their existing practices; people with medical debt and harassed borrowers got no new protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Debt collectors and private student lenders

for.name: Maxine Waters
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill, steered it through committee markup (reported as amended 30-23), and managed it on the House floor.

against.name: 206 of 212 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage; none voted yes.

against.name: Sherrod Brown
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee action or a Senate vote after it was referred to his committee.

against.name: Ann Wagner
against.what_they_did: Offered floor amendments and demanded recorded votes; the amendments were defeated.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost perfectly by party: 215 of 218 voting Democrats yes, 0 of 212 voting Republicans yes, for a final 215-207.

industries.note: The bill bans collecting time-barred debts, limits electronic contact without consent, requires documented ownership of debts before suing, caps fees on government-debt collections at 10 percent, and raises damages for violations. Its revenue depends largely on the practices being restricted, which is why its interest runs against consumers here.

The bill bars reporting debt from medically necessary procedures and delays other medical debt reporting, and requires agencies to remove adverse private student loan information from the COVID period. Medical debt is a large volume of tradeline data, so the bureaus lose data volume while consumers keep cleaner credit files.

Mandatory discharge at death or total permanent disability, cosigner release, and temporary COVID-era credit reporting relief remove both collection leverage and risk transfer to families. Lenders would reprice or tighten underwriting in response.

industries.industry: Lenders using confession-of-judgment clauses (including merchant cash advance firms)
industries.note: The bill bans taking or enforcing waivers of a borrower's right to notice and a day in court, a tool used to seize small business accounts without a hearing. Its main effect is to preserve small business owners' day in court.
